screens.title: Asset Optimization & Memory Management
screens.subtitle: Make builds smaller, reduce runtime memory pressure, and stop GC stutters

narration.text: In this chapter you will learn why asset optimization and memory management are fundamental to a smooth game experience. Unoptimized textures, meshes, and audio quickly bloat build size and consume runtime R A M, which can cause long load times, frequent frame drops, and garbage collection pauses on lower-end hardware. You will see concrete import-setting choices, how to create LODs for models, which audio load types to use, and why mip maps and compression matter. We will also cover Unity’s memory model: how the garbage collector works, what causes allocation spikes, and how object pooling prevents repeated allocations. A practical lab walks you through refactoring a spawning script to use an ObjectPool and verifying the improvement with the Profiler. By the end of this chapter you’ll know how to make targeted changes—reduce a texture’s max size, disable read/write on meshes, choose streaming or decompression for audio, and implement a pool—to reduce GC events and keep steady frame rates. Think about a device with limited R A M: these techniques are what keep your game playable there. Which optimization would you try first in your project?

keyIdea.title: Why this matters
keyIdea.text: Small changes to import settings and memory patterns prevent large runtime stalls and reduce build size, improving playability on all devices.

screens.title: Why asset optimization matters
screens.subtitle: How textures, meshes, and audio affect build size and runtime memory

narration.text: Asset optimization is the deliberate practice of sizing, compressing, and configuring assets so they deliver visual and audio quality where it matters while keeping memory and build sizes small. A single high-resolution texture can occupy megabytes of G P U memory, and thousands of such assets or unnecessarily high import settings add up quickly. Textures should use the smallest resolution and compressed formats that still look acceptable for their use. For meshes, your polygon budget should match the screen space the object occupies; distant props need far fewer triangles. Audio must use sensible load types: short SFX often belong as decompressed in memory for instant playback, while long background music benefits from streaming to avoid occupying R A M. Importantly, some import flags have runtime costs; for example, leaving Read/Write enabled duplicates the mesh data into C P U memory. The practical effect of these choices is visible: smaller texture max sizes lower G P U memory usage and faster loading; lower polygon LODs reduce vertex processing; correct audio load types reduce peak R A M. A useful misconception to check is thinking "higher fidelity always improves perceived quality" — often lower-resolution textures or compressed audio are indistinguishable in context, but dramatically cheaper in memory. By the end of this lesson, you should be able to inspect a problematic asset, choose a lighter import configuration, and predict the runtime effect of that change.

keyIdea.title: Definition
keyIdea.text: Asset optimization balances quality and memory usage by selecting appropriate import settings for textures, meshes, and audio.

content.html:
Module 6 › Chapter 6.4 › Why asset optimization matters
Definition

Optimize assets to control memory and build size

Small changes to import settings yield large savings in RAM and reduce startup and runtime stalls.

Texture example
Background prop: drop from 4K to 512 or 1024 and enable Mip Maps. Use ASTC/ETC for mobile or DXT on desktop.
Mesh example
Convert a distant 50k polygon model to LODs: 10k for medium distance, 2k for far distance to cut GPU vertex work.
Audio example
Short impact SFX: Decompress on Load. Long music: Stream from disk to avoid high RAM usage.
Key Takeaway

Match asset fidelity to screen space and use compression and streaming to reduce memory without harming visible quality.

Practical checklist
  • Inspect large textures; reduce Max Size where detail is unnecessary.
  • Enable Mip Maps for 3D textures to save GPU memory when distant.
  • Disable Read/Write unless runtime mesh access is required.
  • Add LOD groups to complex models to reduce vertex work at distance.
  • Choose audio load type based on clip length and frequency of playback.
Common misconception
Higher resolution always improves perceived quality. In many cases, properly compressed and sized assets are visually indistinguishable but far cheaper in memory.

screens.title: Texture optimization process
screens.subtitle: Resolution, compression, and mip maps — a practical workflow

narration.text: Optimizing textures is a repeatable process that reduces G P U memory without sacrificing the look where it matters. Start by auditing textures in the Project window and sort by size to find the largest offenders. For each texture ask: where is this used and how large does it appear on screen? If it’s a tiny prop seen at distance, drop the Max Size to 512 or 1024. Next, choose compression: on desktop DXT formats are common, while mobile benefits from ETC or ASTC. Apply Normal Map compression for normal maps specifically, and reserve RGBA 32-bit for UI elements that require full alpha clarity. Then decide on Mip Maps: for any 3D textured object that can appear at variable distances, enable Generate Mip Maps so the G P U uses smaller versions when appropriate. Finally, test in the Scene and check the Memory usage in the Profiler. A concrete example: a background rock texture imported at 4K can be reduced to 1024, compressed to ASTC (mobile) or DXT (desktop), and still look the same at distance while releasing several megabytes of VRAM. A common mistake is leaving everything at source resolution; another is over-compressing UI sprites, which can make text look soft. The step-by-step approach helps you trade memory and fidelity consciously.

keyIdea.title: Workflow
keyIdea.text: Audit large textures, choose appropriate max size and compression, enable Mip Maps for 3D usage, and verify memory in the Profiler.

content.html:
Module 6 › Chapter 6.4 › Texture optimization
Step-by-step
  1. Audit Project window and sort by asset size to find largest textures.
  2. Decide screen-space need and set Max Size accordingly (e.g., 512, 1024).
  3. Choose Compression format for target platform (DXT / ETC / ASTC).
  4. Enable Generate Mip Maps for 3D use to save GPU memory when distant.
  5. Test in-scene, use the Profiler Memory to confirm savings.
Concrete example
A 4K foliage texture used at distance can be lowered to 1024, compressed to ASTC, and still appear identical in-game while freeing VRAM and lowering build size.
Supporting notes
  • Normal maps need normal-specific import settings; treat them separately.
  • UI elements sometimes require higher bit depth for crisp alpha; balance that with memory budget.
  • Use platform overrides in Import Settings to set different formats for mobile and desktop.
Key Takeaway

Apply the smallest acceptable texture sizes and platform-appropriate compression, and rely on mip maps for distant geometry.

screens.title: Meshes and LOD strategy
screens.subtitle: Balancing polygon count and performance using LOD groups

narration.text: Meshes directly affect G P U and C P U work through vertex processing and draw calls. The goal is to use the lowest polygon count that preserves visual fidelity at the distance the model will be viewed. Start by examining where the model appears and how large it is on screen. If it's a distant environmental asset, create decimated versions with tools like Blender and add them as LOD levels in Unity using an LOD Group component. LODs let Unity swap to simpler meshes when the camera distance exceeds configured thresholds, reducing vertex count and improving frame rates. Also disable Read/Write on imported meshes unless you need to access vertex data at runtime; leaving it enabled duplicates mesh data into C P U memory. A common misconception is that a single highly detailed mesh is fine because modern GPUs are fast; however, many objects with high vertex counts multiply the work and can bottleneck mobile and low-end hardware. An example: a building seen from far away can use a 50k model at near range, but 10k and 2k LODs for medium and far distances will dramatically lower processing while retaining silhouette. Finally, verify in the Scene view and profile the scene to ensure LOD transitions are clean and performance improves.

keyIdea.title: LOD principle
keyIdea.text: Swap to simpler meshes based on camera distance to reduce vertex work without harming perceived quality.

content.html:
Module 6 › Chapter 6.4 › Meshes & LOD
Why it matters

Reduce vertex processing with LODs

Use multiple mesh resolutions and let Unity swap them based on distance to save GPU work.

Practical steps
Create decimated LODs in your modeling tool, import them, and assign to an LOD Group component with appropriate screen-relative thresholds.
Import tip
Uncheck Read/Write for models that won’t be modified at runtime to avoid CPU memory duplication.
Comparison
Single high-detail mesh
Simple to manage but wastes vertex processing on distant objects and can duplicate memory if Read/Write is enabled.
LOD group with 3 levels
Swaps meshes by distance, reducing GPU load while preserving the appearance at relevant ranges.
Key Takeaway

Use LODs and disable unnecessary Read/Write to reduce both GPU and CPU memory usage while maintaining visuals where they matter.

screens.title: Memory management and garbage collection
screens.subtitle: How Unity's managed memory and GC affect gameplay

narration.text: Unity runs on a managed environment where the C# garbage collector automatically reclaims memory that no longer has live references. While this relieves you from manual deallocation, it also introduces pauses when the collector runs, especially if many allocations have occurred. The common pattern that triggers GC issues is creating many short-lived objects inside frequently called loops such as Update, for example repeatedly calling new List or instantiating temporary objects. Each allocation increases managed heap usage and eventually forces a GC. These pauses are visible as frame stutters and are worst on platforms with limited C P U resources. To reason about this, think of memory allocation as a faucet: uncontrolled flow fills the sink faster and forces a big clean-up. The practical counter is to avoid allocations in hot paths: reuse containers, avoid boxing, cache references, and use object pooling for recurring entities. A common misconception is that small allocations are harmless; in aggregate they can accumulate and trigger costly GC runs. Use the Unity Profiler to monitor GC. Collect events and the Memory timeline so you can see which code paths allocate the most. The reward for applying these practices is smoother, more predictable frame timing.

keyIdea.title: Memory fact
keyIdea.text: Garbage collection reclaims unreferenced memory, but frequent allocations in hot loops create noticeable pauses.

content.html:
Module 6 › Chapter 6.4 › Memory management
Concept

Garbage Collector basics

The GC automatically frees memory for objects that are no longer referenced. Large or frequent allocations cause pauses when the GC runs.

Example allocation pitfall
Creating new collections or strings inside Update every frame adds many short-lived objects that trigger GC.Collect.
Mitigations
  • Reuse collections and buffers instead of newing them.
  • Avoid boxing and use structs carefully.
  • Implement object pooling for high-frequency GameObjects.
Detecting GC issues

Open the Profiler and watch for GC.Collect spikes in CPU Usage and Memory allocation growth in the Memory module. Correlate spikes with gameplay actions.

Common mistake

Assuming GC spikes are only caused by huge single allocations. Often many small allocations add up quickly.

screens.title: Object Pooling example
screens.subtitle: A practical ObjectPool implementation to avoid Instantiate/Destroy

narration.text: Object pooling is a simple but powerful design pattern for reducing runtime allocations. Instead of creating and destroying objects repeatedly, you pre-create a collection of objects and reuse them. The core idea is creating a pool, borrowing objects by activating and initializing them, and returning them by deactivating and resetting state. The provided ObjectPool. cs creates a Queue of GameObjects in Awake and prepares them inactive. When an object is needed, GetPooledObject dequeues and activates one; when finished, ReturnPooledObject deactivates and enqueues it. This approach prevents Instantiate and Destroy calls during gameplay and cuts down managed allocations that lead to GC spikes. A concrete example is bullets fired rapidly: the pool holds a limited number of bullet instances and reuses them each shot. A common pitfall is failing to reset all runtime state, which can lead to unexpected behavior; always initialize position, velocity, and any timers when you borrow an object. Another risk is exhausting the pool; decide whether to log and expand or to block. Use the Profiler before and after the change to observe reduced GC events during intense firing. Practice: paste the code in a script, attach it to an empty GameObject, and hook your spawning logic to GetPooledObject and ReturnPooledObject.

keyIdea.title: Pattern summary
keyIdea.text: Pre-create objects and reuse them to avoid runtime allocations and reduce GC pressure.

content.html:
Module 6 › Chapter 6.4 › Object Pooling
ObjectPool.cs
using System.Collections.Generic;
using UnityEngine;

public class ObjectPool : MonoBehaviour
{
    public GameObject prefab;
    public int poolSize = 10;
    private Queue<GameObject> _pool = new Queue<GameObject>();

    void Awake()
    {
        for (int i = 0; i < poolSize; i++)
        {
            GameObject obj = Instantiate(prefab);
            obj.transform.SetParent(this.transform);
            obj.SetActive(false);
            _pool.Enqueue(obj);
        }
    }

    public GameObject GetPooledObject()
    {
        if (_pool.Count > 0)
        {
            GameObject obj = _pool.Dequeue();
            obj.SetActive(true);
            return obj;
        }
        else
        {
            Debug.LogWarning("Pool exhausted! Instantiating new object.");
            GameObject obj = Instantiate(prefab);
            obj.transform.SetParent(this.transform);
            return obj;
        }
    }

    public void ReturnPooledObject(GameObject obj)
    {
        obj.SetActive(false);
        _pool.Enqueue(obj);
    }
}
Explanation
  • The pool pre-instantiates objects in Awake and keeps them inactive until needed.
  • GetPooledObject returns an object and activates it; ReturnPooledObject deactivates and re-enqueues it.
  • Decide whether to expand the pool or warn if exhausted to avoid runtime surprises.
  • Always reset object state when borrowed to avoid leftover data from previous usage.
Check your understanding

Why does pooling reduce GC spikes compared to Instantiate/Destroy? Answer: it avoids repeated allocations and deallocations during gameplay.

screens.title: Instantiate/Destroy vs Object Pooling
screens.subtitle: Trade-offs and when to expand a pool

narration.text: Comparing Instantiate/Destroy with object pooling helps make the trade-offs clear. Instantiate and Destroy are simple: create an object when needed and remove it when done. This is easy for one-off, rare objects, but with frequent creation and destruction you generate many managed allocations and corresponding GC activity. Object pooling costs memory upfront because you allocate a pool, but it keeps runtime allocations low by reusing objects. This pattern drastically reduces GC spikes for frequently used entities like bullets, particle bursts, and spawned enemies. However, pooling requires careful state management: you must reset position, velocity, and other state when reusing an object, and you must ensure returned objects do not retain references that prevent them from being garbage collected if the entire pool should be released. Pool exhaustion is another design decision: you can either log and expand the pool dynamically or cap the count and reuse the oldest object. A common misconception is that pooling always reduces memory usage; in fact it increases steady memory usage but improves runtime stability and frame consistency. Use the Profiler to compare before and after: look for lower peak allocations and fewer GC. Collect events during high activity.

keyIdea.title: Trade-off
keyIdea.text: Pooling trades higher baseline memory for fewer runtime allocations and smoother frame timing during high-frequency object usage.

content.html:
Module 6 › Chapter 6.4 › Instantiate vs Pooling
Instantiate / Destroy
Simple, minimal upfront memory, but creates allocations each use. Best for rare or unique objects.
Problems under load
Many Instantiate/Destroy cycles cause frequent GC.Collect spikes and frame stutter.
Object Pooling
Higher baseline memory, minimal allocations during gameplay, and more consistent frame times. Best for bullets, particles, and common spawnable objects.
Design choices
Decide on pool size, expansion policy, and thorough state reset when returning objects to the pool.
Check your understanding

When would you prefer Instantiate/Destroy over pooling? Answer: for rare or unique objects where pooling overhead isn't justified.

screens.title: Refactor spawning to use a pool
screens.subtitle: PlayerShootingOptimized and BulletBehavior integration

narration.text: Refactoring a spawning script to use an ObjectPool is a focused change that yields immediate benefits. The optimized PlayerShooting script replaces Instantiate with a GetPooledObject call and positions the returned object at the fire point. The bullet’s behavior script needs a SetPool method and an Activate method to reset timers and state. When a bullet expires or collides, it calls ReturnPooledObject to go back into the pool instead of Destroy. Concrete code examples show the pattern: the shooter asks the pool for an object, initializes transform and velocity, and the bullet internally returns itself after a lifetime or on collision. A common pitfall is forgetting to assign the pool reference on the prefab or failing to reset movement vectors and damage states, leading to reused bullets behaving like their last use. Also be mindful of pool setup in Awake versus Start so all pools exist before gameplay begins. After refactoring, run the scene under the Profiler to compare memory allocation and GC events during intense firing. The expected result is fewer allocations and fewer GC spikes, producing smoother gameplay during rapid fire sequences.

keyIdea.title: Refactor strategy
keyIdea.text: Replace Instantiate with GetPooledObject, initialize state, and ensure bullets call ReturnPooledObject on expiry or collision.

content.html:
Module 6 › Chapter 6.4 › Refactor spawning
PlayerShootingOptimized
using UnityEngine;

public class PlayerShootingOptimized : MonoBehaviour
{
    public ObjectPool bulletPool; // Assign ObjectPool component
    public Transform firePoint;
    public float fireRate = 0.5f;
    private float nextFireTime;

    void Update()
    {
        if (Time.time >= nextFireTime && Input.GetButtonDown("Fire1"))
        {
            GameObject bullet = bulletPool.GetPooledObject();
            if (bullet != null)
            {
                bullet.transform.position = firePoint.position;
                bullet.transform.rotation = firePoint.rotation;
                // Initialize bullet state here
                BulletBehavior bb = bullet.GetComponent<BulletBehavior>();
                if (bb != null)
                {
                    bb.SetPool(bulletPool);
                    bb.Activate();
                }
            }
            nextFireTime = Time.time + fireRate;
        }
    }
}
BulletBehavior (return to pool)
using UnityEngine;

public class BulletBehavior : MonoBehaviour
{
    private ObjectPool _myPool;
    public float lifetime = 3f;
    private float _activeTime;

    public void SetPool(ObjectPool pool){ _myPool = pool; }

    public void Activate(){ _activeTime = 0f; /* reset other state */ }

    void Update()
    {
        _activeTime += Time.deltaTime;
        if (_activeTime >= lifetime) ReturnToPool();
    }

    void OnCollisionEnter(Collision collision)
    {
        // collision handling
        ReturnToPool();
    }

    void ReturnToPool()
    {
        if (_myPool != null)
        {
            _myPool.ReturnPooledObject(this.gameObject);
        }
        else
        {
            Destroy(this.gameObject);
        }
    }
}
Notes
  • Always reset state in Activate to avoid leftover values.
  • Assign the pool reference to prefabs or set it at spawn time.
  • Test for pool exhaustion behavior under peak load.

screens.title: Spotting memory leaks and using the Profiler
screens.subtitle: Common leak causes and how to confirm them

narration.text: Even in a garbage-collected environment like Unity, memory leaks happen when objects remain referenced but are no longer needed. Common sources are unsubscribed events where the publisher keeps a delegate reference to a destroyed subscriber, static references that unintentionally hold scene objects, and coroutines that never stop. To detect leaks, use the Unity Profiler’s Memory tab and take snapshots before and after scene transitions or repeated actions. Look for objects that remain allocated across snapshots when they should have been freed. The Profiler also shows managed heap sizes and can point to retained objects and their types. A practical example: if you find many instances of a particular MonoBehaviour are still present after unloading a scene, inspect static fields and event subscriptions in that class. Always unsubscribe from events in OnDestroy or use weak event patterns where appropriate. Coroutines should be explicitly stopped when an object is disabled or destroyed. The payoff for finding and fixing leaks is reliable memory usage over long play sessions, preventing gradual R A M growth that eventually causes crashes or out-of-memory conditions. End with a simple check: does reloading the scene increase memory across multiple loads? If so, you likely have a leak to find.

keyIdea.title: Leak indicators
keyIdea.text: Held references, unsubscribed events, static fields, and active coroutines commonly prevent GC from collecting unused objects.

content.html:
Module 6 › Chapter 6.4 › Detecting leaks
Common causes
Unsubscribed events
Publishers retain delegates to destroyed subscribers, preventing collection.
Static references
Static fields holding scene objects keep them alive across scene changes.
Stuck coroutines
Coroutines that never finish can keep references alive indefinitely.
Profiler workflow
  1. Run a scenario that should release objects (scene unload or repeated spawn cycles).
  2. Take Memory snapshots before and after the scenario.
  3. Compare snapshots for objects that persist unexpectedly and inspect retaining paths.
Real-world check

Reload the same scene several times and watch total memory. If it rises each load, investigate retained references and unsubscribe or clear statics as needed.

screens.title: Lab: Implement object pooling and verify in Profiler
screens.subtitle: Step-by-step refactor and profiler validation

narration.text: This hands-on activity walks you through implementing object pooling for a frequent object, such as a bullet, then verifying the improvement with the Unity Profiler. First, identify a GameObject that is frequently instantiated and destroyed. Next, create an empty GameObject named ObjectPoolManager and attach the supplied ObjectPool. cs script. Assign your bullet prefab to the pool and set an initial pool size appropriate for expected simultaneous objects. Third, modify your spawning script to call GetPooledObject instead of Instantiate and initialize the returned object, as shown in the PlayerShootingOptimized example. Ensure each pooled prefab contains a behavior that calls ReturnPooledObject on lifetime expiry or collision. Fourth, run the scene with the Profiler open and capture C P U and Memory traces while firing rapidly. Observe GC. Collect spikes and allocation rates before the change, then repeat after pooling is active. You should see fewer allocations and less frequent GC spikes. A debugging tip: if bullets misbehave when reused, double-check Reset/Activate logic. Finally, reflect: did the change reduce GC events as expected? If not, repeat the Profiler trace and inspect which allocations still occur.

keyIdea.title: Lab goal
keyIdea.text: Refactor spawning to use pooling and confirm lower allocations and fewer GC spikes using the Profiler.

Choose a frequently created object like a bullet or particle effect.

3. Refactor spawner

  2. Apply pooling and capture the same scenario again.
  3. Compare allocation graphs and GC events; you should see fewer allocations and less frequent GC spikes.
Pro tip

If pooling doesn't reduce GC, inspect other allocations in the profiled timeline; temporary collections, string allocations, or other systems may still allocate heavily.

screens.title: Optimization checklist & common mistakes
screens.subtitle: A compact checklist to keep your project memory-friendly

narration.text: This checklist collects the most effective, repeatable practices for keeping build size and runtime memory manageable. First, audit assets and reduce texture Max Size where detail is unnecessary, enabling Mip Maps for 3D uses. Second, apply platform-specific compression settings in Import Settings so mobile and desktop use appropriate formats. Third, create LODs for complex models and disable Read/Write when not required. Fourth, choose audio load types: Decompress On Load for short, latency-sensitive sounds and Streaming for long music tracks. Fifth, avoid allocations in hot paths by reusing collections and buffers and by avoiding boxing. Sixth, implement object pooling for bullets, particles, and frequent spawns, and ensure reuse resets state fully. Seventh, guard against memory leaks by unsubscribing events, clearing statics, and stopping coroutines when objects are destroyed. Finally, verify every change with the Profiler’s Memory and C P U views. A common mistake is optimizing blindly—make one change, measure it, and iterate. This disciplined approach ensures you improve performance without sacrificing necessary visual or audio quality. Optimization checklist & common mistakes means audit, adjust import settings, use lods, pick audio load types, avoid runtime allocations, pool frequent objects, and verify with the profiler.. In practical terms, a compact checklist to keep your project memory-friendly. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Checklist
keyIdea.text: Audit, adjust import settings, use LODs, pick audio load types, avoid runtime allocations, pool frequent objects, and verify with the Profiler.

content.html:
Module 6 › Chapter 6.4 › Checklist

Optimization checklist

Audit large textures and reduce Max Size where possible.
Enable Mip Maps for 3D textures to save GPU memory.
Use platform-appropriate compression formats (DXT, ETC, ASTC).
Create LODs and disable Read/Write unless needed at runtime.
Choose audio load types: Decompress On Load for SFX, Streaming for music.
Avoid allocations in Update; reuse collections and buffers.
Implement and test object pooling for frequent spawns.
Unsubscribe events, clear statics, and stop coroutines to prevent leaks.
Key Takeaway

Measure before and after each change using the Profiler to ensure real gains and avoid over-optimizing where it isn't needed.

screens.title: Key Concepts
screens.subtitle: What to remember from this chapter

narration.text: These are the concise ideas you should carry forward. Asset Optimization means matching fidelity to need and using compression and import settings to reduce memory and build size. Texture Compression and Mip Maps let the G P U use smaller texture levels at distance, saving VRAM and improving performance. LODs swap complex meshes for simpler ones far from the camera to reduce vertex processing. These techniques together shrink the runtime footprint and keep your rendering stable. Commit these concepts to memory: small, target-appropriate textures, LODs for complex meshes, and sensible audio load choices often yield the biggest wins. screens.subtitle: Three core concepts to apply immediately

narration.text: Keep these three practical ideas at the center of your optimization work. First, import settings are your most immediate leverage: use reduced Max Size, compression, and mip maps to cut memory at the source. Second, runtime allocation patterns determine smoothness: avoid creating garbage in hot loops and prefer reuse for frequent objects. Third, use the Profiler as your single source of truth—measure memory and GC events before and after changes to confirm improvements. These are the habits that turn occasional optimization into a reliable workflow for shipping playable builds across devices. ai_generation_note: Design an 11-minute interactive lab. Start by showing a Unity scene with a simple script that `Instantiate`s and `Destroy`s many objects (e.g., bullets) rapidly. Open the Profiler and highlight the "GC.Collect" spikes in the CPU Usage and Memory sections. Then, guide the learner through creating an `ObjectPool` script and refactoring the spawning script to use the pool. After the refactor, run the scene again and show the Profiler, demonstrating the significant reduction in GC spikes. Include side-by-side code views of the before/after spawning logic. The interactive element should be a short coding challenge to implement the `ReturnPooledObject` method in the `BulletBehavior` script.
